```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(scales)
library(broom)
library(knitr)

data_candidates <- c(
  "Data/owid-co2-data.csv",
  "data/owid-co2-data.csv",
  "../data/owid-co2-data.csv",
  "../Data/owid-co2-data.csv"
)
co2_path <- data_candidates[file.exists(data_candidates)][1]

if (is.na(co2_path)) {
  stop("Could not find owid-co2-data.csv in Report/Data, Report/data, ../data or ../Data.")
}

co2_raw <- read_csv(co2_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

co2_countries <- co2_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(iso_code), !str_starts(iso_code, "OWID")) |>
  mutate(
    carbon_intensity = if_else(gdp > 0, co2 / gdp * 1e12, NA_real_),
    coal_share = if_else(co2 > 0, coal_co2 / co2, NA_real_),
    oil_share = if_else(co2 > 0, oil_co2 / co2, NA_real_),
    gas_share = if_else(co2 > 0, gas_co2 / co2, NA_real_),
    cement_share = if_else(co2 > 0, cement_co2 / co2, NA_real_)
  )

latest_year <- 2022
growth_start <- 2012

focus_target <- c("Indonesia", "Vietnam", "India")
focus_benchmark <- c("Australia", "Japan", "South Korea")
focus_all <- c(focus_target, focus_benchmark)

growth_10yr <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(growth_start, latest_year)) |>
  select(country, iso_code, year, co2) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = co2,
    names_prefix = "co2_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    co2_growth_10yr_pct =
      (co2_2022 - co2_2012) / co2_2012 * 100
  ) |>
  select(country, iso_code, co2_growth_10yr_pct)

intensity_change <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(growth_start, latest_year)) |>
  select(country, year, carbon_intensity) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = year,
    values_from = carbon_intensity,
    names_prefix = "intensity_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    intensity_change_pct =
      (intensity_2022 - intensity_2012) / intensity_2012 * 100
  ) |>
  select(country, intensity_change_pct)

latest_panel_all <- co2_countries |>
  filter(
    year == latest_year,
    !is.na(carbon_intensity),
    !is.na(coal_share),
    !is.na(co2)
  ) |>
  left_join(growth_10yr, by = c("country", "iso_code")) |>
  left_join(intensity_change, by = "country")

latest_panel_focus <- latest_panel_all |>
  filter(country %in% focus_all) |>
  mutate(
    role = case_when(
      country %in% c("Indonesia", "Vietnam") ~ "Primary target",
      country == "India" ~ "Supporting case",
      TRUE ~ "Benchmark"
    ),
    recent_trend = case_when(
      country == "Vietnam" ~ "Intensity rising again",
      country == "Indonesia" ~ "Only slight decoupling",
      country == "India" ~ "Partial decoupling",
      country == "Australia" ~ "Strong decoupling",
      country == "Japan" ~ "Strong decoupling",
      country == "South Korea" ~ "Strong decoupling",
      TRUE ~ "Mixed"
    ),
    priority_level = case_when(
      country %in% c("Indonesia", "Vietnam") ~ "Primary target",
      country == "India" ~ "Supporting case",
      TRUE ~ "Benchmark"
    )
  )

priority_labels <- tribble(
  ~country,        ~label_x, ~label_y,
  "Vietnam",       374,      118,
  "India",         304,       62,
  "Indonesia",     168,       68,
  "Australia",     338,      -18,
  "Japan",         238,      -30,
  "South Korea",   352,       10
)

priority_plot_data <- latest_panel_focus |>
  left_join(priority_labels, by = "country")

trend_data <- co2_countries |>
  filter(
    country %in% focus_all,
    year >= 1990,
    year <= latest_year,
    !is.na(carbon_intensity)
  )

trend_label_offsets <- tribble(
  ~country,        ~offset,
  "Vietnam",          12,
  "India",           -12,
  "Indonesia",        14,
  "Australia",        -8,
  "Japan",            -6,
  "South Korea",      13
)

trend_labels <- trend_data |>
  group_by(country) |>
  filter(year == max(year)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(trend_label_offsets, by = "country") |>
  mutate(
    label_x = latest_year + 1.4,
    label_y = carbon_intensity + offset
  )

fuel_wide <- latest_panel_focus |>
  transmute(
    country,
    Coal = coal_share,
    Oil = oil_share,
    Gas = gas_share,
    Cement = cement_share
  )

fuel_order <- fuel_wide |>
  arrange(desc(Coal)) |>
  pull(country)

fuel_long <- fuel_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    -country,
    names_to = "source",
    values_to = "share"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(share)) |>
  mutate(
    source = factor(source, levels = c("Coal", "Oil", "Gas", "Cement")),
    country = factor(country, levels = rev(fuel_order))
  )

coal_labels <- fuel_wide |>
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = rev(fuel_order)))

priority_table_display <- latest_panel_focus |>
  arrange(factor(country, levels = c("Indonesia", "Vietnam", "India",
                                     "Australia", "Japan", "South Korea"))) |>
  transmute(
    Country = country,
    `Carbon intensity (t / M 2011 PPP$)` = number(carbon_intensity, accuracy = 1),
    `Recent trend` = recent_trend,
    `Coal share` = percent(coal_share, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Priority level` = case_when(
      priority_level == "Primary target" ~
        "<span class='priority-pill priority-pill--high'>Primary target</span>",
      priority_level == "Supporting case" ~
        "<span class='priority-pill priority-pill--support'>Supporting case</span>",
      TRUE ~
        "<span class='priority-pill priority-pill--benchmark'>Benchmark</span>"
    )
  )

reg_data <- latest_panel_all |>
  filter(
    !is.na(carbon_intensity),
    carbon_intensity > 0,
    !is.na(coal_share),
    coal_share >= 0,
    coal_share <= 1
  )

# Sample-composition transparency (surfaced in Data Preparation Notes)
n_2022_country_rows <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year == latest_year) |> nrow()
n_panel_all        <- nrow(latest_panel_all)
n_reg_data         <- nrow(reg_data)
n_dropped_to_reg   <- n_panel_all - n_reg_data

fit <- lm(log(carbon_intensity) ~ coal_share, data = reg_data)
fit_summary <- summary(fit)
fit_tidy <- tidy(fit)
fit_glance <- glance(fit)

beta1 <- fit_tidy |> filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(estimate)
beta1_se <- fit_tidy |> filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(std.error)
beta1_p <- fit_tidy |> filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(p.value)
beta1_t <- fit_tidy |> filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(statistic)
r_sq <- fit_glance$r.squared
assoc_10pp <- (exp(beta1 * 0.10) - 1) * 100
shapiro_p <- shapiro.test(residuals(fit))$p.value

benchmark_mean_intensity <- latest_panel_focus |>
  filter(country %in% focus_benchmark) |>
  summarise(value = mean(carbon_intensity, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(value)

top_total_emitters <- latest_panel_all |>
  arrange(desc(co2)) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  pull(country)

# ============================================================================
# Robustness datasets (Phase A — data prep only; existing figures unchanged)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three additional analytical frames that will feed the planned robustness
# checks (results not yet rendered to figures or tables):
#   1. growth_model_data           — does 10-yr CO2 growth track 10-yr GDP
#                                    growth once coal share is included?
#   2. intensity_change_model_data — does Δ carbon intensity (2012 → 2022)
#                                    track Δ coal share over the same window?
#   3. multivariate_2022_data      — does the coal-share slope on log(carbon
#                                    intensity) survive controlling for log
#                                    GDP per capita in the 2022 cross-section?
# Each frame is built tidyverse-style off `co2_countries` and the existing
# `growth_10yr` / `intensity_change` helpers, so nothing upstream is mutated.
# ============================================================================

# ---- Shared building blocks ------------------------------------------------

# 2012 → 2022 GDP growth, mirroring the shape of `growth_10yr`
gdp_growth_10yr <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(growth_start, latest_year),
         !is.na(gdp), gdp > 0) |>
  select(country, iso_code, year, gdp) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from   = year,
    values_from  = gdp,
    names_prefix = "gdp_"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(gdp_2012), !is.na(gdp_2022), gdp_2012 > 0) |>
  mutate(gdp_growth_10yr_pct = (gdp_2022 - gdp_2012) / gdp_2012 * 100) |>
  select(country, iso_code, gdp_growth_10yr_pct)

# 2022 coal share — used as a structural covariate in the growth model
coal_share_2022 <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year == latest_year,
         !is.na(coal_share),
         coal_share >= 0, coal_share <= 1) |>
  select(country, iso_code, coal_share)

# 2012 → 2022 coal-share change in percentage points (Δ coal share × 100)
coal_share_change <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(growth_start, latest_year)) |>
  select(country, iso_code, year, coal_share) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from   = year,
    values_from  = coal_share,
    names_prefix = "coal_"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(coal_2012), !is.na(coal_2022),
         coal_2012 >= 0, coal_2012 <= 1,
         coal_2022 >= 0, coal_2022 <= 1) |>
  mutate(coal_share_change_pp = (coal_2022 - coal_2012) * 100) |>
  select(country, iso_code, coal_share_change_pp)

# ---- 1. Growth-model dataset ----------------------------------------------
# 10-year CO2 growth + 10-year GDP growth + 2022 coal share, on every country
# with complete data on all three columns. Drops NA / Inf.
growth_model_data <- growth_10yr |>
  inner_join(gdp_growth_10yr, by = c("country", "iso_code")) |>
  inner_join(coal_share_2022, by = c("country", "iso_code")) |>
  filter(
    is.finite(co2_growth_10yr_pct),
    is.finite(gdp_growth_10yr_pct),
    is.finite(coal_share)
  )

# ---- 2. Intensity-change-model dataset ------------------------------------
# Δ carbon intensity (2012 → 2022, %) + Δ coal share (2012 → 2022, pp).
# `intensity_change` upstream has only `country`, so the join key is country.
intensity_change_model_data <- intensity_change |>
  inner_join(coal_share_change, by = "country") |>
  filter(
    is.finite(intensity_change_pct),
    is.finite(coal_share_change_pp)
  )

# ---- 3. Multivariate 2022 intensity dataset -------------------------------
# 2022 cross-section with carbon intensity, coal share, and GDP per capita.
# log(carbon_intensity) and log(gdp_per_capita) are the intended response /
# control in the planned multivariate regression, so non-positive values are
# excluded here at the data-prep stage.
multivariate_2022_data <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year == latest_year,
         !is.na(carbon_intensity), carbon_intensity > 0,
         !is.na(coal_share),       coal_share >= 0, coal_share <= 1,
         !is.na(gdp),              gdp > 0,
         !is.na(population),       population > 0) |>
  mutate(gdp_per_capita = gdp / population) |>
  filter(is.finite(gdp_per_capita), gdp_per_capita > 0) |>
  select(country, iso_code,
         carbon_intensity, coal_share,
         gdp, population, gdp_per_capita)

# ---- Pre-COVID growth (2010 → 2019), built parallel to growth_10yr ---------
# Used in Appendix 2 robustness tab to test whether Vietnam's +106% headline
# is partly a COVID-rebound artifact (2020-21 demand recovery).
precovid_start <- 2010
precovid_end   <- 2019

co2_growth_precovid <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(precovid_start, precovid_end)) |>
  select(country, iso_code, year, co2) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from   = year,
    values_from  = co2,
    names_prefix = "co2_"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_2010), !is.na(co2_2019), co2_2010 > 0) |>
  mutate(co2_growth_precovid_pct = (co2_2019 - co2_2010) / co2_2010 * 100) |>
  select(country, iso_code, co2_growth_precovid_pct)

# Combine both growth windows for the focus six (drives the comparison chart)
focus_growth_compare <- latest_panel_focus |>
  transmute(country, iso_code, role = priority_level,
            growth_2012_2022 = co2_growth_10yr_pct) |>
  left_join(co2_growth_precovid, by = c("country", "iso_code"))

# ============================================================================
# Robustness regressions (Phase A — three supplementary models)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three additional OLS fits that probe whether the headline coal–intensity
# signal in the Hypothesis Test section survives different cuts of the same data. Each
# model is associational; none claims causation. Inline scalars are pulled
# out for the Robustness Checks section.
# ============================================================================

# ---- 1. Growth model: 10-yr CO2 growth ~ coal share + 10-yr GDP growth ----
growth_fit         <- lm(co2_growth_10yr_pct ~ coal_share + gdp_growth_10yr_pct,
                         data = growth_model_data)
growth_fit_tidy    <- broom::tidy(growth_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
growth_fit_glance  <- broom::glance(growth_fit)

growth_coal_beta   <- growth_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(estimate)
growth_coal_p      <- growth_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(p.value)
growth_gdp_beta    <- growth_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "gdp_growth_10yr_pct") |> pull(estimate)
growth_gdp_p       <- growth_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "gdp_growth_10yr_pct") |> pull(p.value)
growth_r_sq        <- growth_fit_glance$r.squared

# ---- 2. Intensity-change model: Δ intensity (%) ~ Δ coal share (pp) -------
change_fit         <- lm(intensity_change_pct ~ coal_share_change_pp,
                         data = intensity_change_model_data)
change_fit_tidy    <- broom::tidy(change_fit, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
change_fit_glance  <- broom::glance(change_fit)

change_coal_beta   <- change_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share_change_pp") |> pull(estimate)
change_coal_p      <- change_fit_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share_change_pp") |> pull(p.value)
change_r_sq        <- change_fit_glance$r.squared

# ---- 3. Multivariate intensity: log(intensity) ~ coal share + log(GDP/cap)
intensity_fit_multivar         <- lm(
  log(carbon_intensity) ~ coal_share + log(gdp_per_capita),
  data = multivariate_2022_data
)
intensity_fit_multivar_tidy    <- broom::tidy(intensity_fit_multivar,
                                              conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)
intensity_fit_multivar_glance  <- broom::glance(intensity_fit_multivar)

mv_coal_beta       <- intensity_fit_multivar_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(estimate)
mv_coal_p          <- intensity_fit_multivar_tidy |>
  filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(p.value)
mv_gdpcap_beta     <- intensity_fit_multivar_tidy |>
  filter(term == "log(gdp_per_capita)") |> pull(estimate)
mv_gdpcap_p        <- intensity_fit_multivar_tidy |>
  filter(term == "log(gdp_per_capita)") |> pull(p.value)
mv_r_sq            <- intensity_fit_multivar_glance$r.squared

# Headline-vs-multivariate slope shrinkage on coal_share (for inline narrative)
mv_coal_shrinkage_pct <- (1 - mv_coal_beta / beta1) * 100

# ============================================================================
# ============================================================================
# Rule-based priority validation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The hardcoded `priority_level` above is the editorial focus-six choice.
# This block defines a transparent rule on (coal_share, co2_growth_10yr_pct)
# and verifies that, applied to the same six countries, the rule produces an
# identical assignment. It also applies the rule to the full 2022 cross-
# section to show how many countries world-wide it would classify the same
# way, defending the priority call against "why these six?" objections.
# ============================================================================

apply_priority_rule <- function(df) {
  df |> mutate(priority_rule = case_when(
    coal_share >= 0.60                                       ~ "Supporting case",
    coal_share >= 0.40 & coal_share < 0.60 &
      !is.na(co2_growth_10yr_pct) & co2_growth_10yr_pct > 0  ~ "Primary target",
    TRUE                                                     ~ "Benchmark"
  ))
}

# Validation: applied to the focus six, the rule must match the editorial pick
focus_rule_check <- latest_panel_focus |>
  apply_priority_rule() |>
  transmute(country, priority_level, priority_rule,
            match = priority_level == priority_rule)
rule_matches_editorial <- all(focus_rule_check$match)

# World application: how many countries fall in each rule bucket?
world_rule <- latest_panel_all |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_growth_10yr_pct), !is.na(coal_share)) |>
  apply_priority_rule()

n_world_primary    <- world_rule |> filter(priority_rule == "Primary target")  |> nrow()
n_world_supporting <- world_rule |> filter(priority_rule == "Supporting case") |> nrow()
n_world_total      <- nrow(world_rule)

# ============================================================================
# Counterfactual transition gap (signature analytical move)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Translates the multivariate intensity model into a decision-relevant number:
# "if a focus economy's coal share matched the three-benchmark average, holding
# its own GDP per capita fixed, how much would the model predict carbon
# intensity to fall?" The gap between the model's prediction at the country's
# *current* coal share and at the *benchmark* coal share quantifies the
# intensity-reduction lever encoded in coal-share targeting alone — a model-
# implied translation, NOT an empirical projection.
# ============================================================================

# Reference coal share = 2022 mean of Australia / Japan / South Korea
benchmark_mean_coal_share <- latest_panel_focus |>
  filter(country %in% focus_benchmark) |>
  summarise(value = mean(coal_share, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(value)

counterfactual_data <- latest_panel_focus |>
  left_join(
    multivariate_2022_data |> select(country, gdp_per_capita),
    by = "country"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    country, role = priority_level,
    coal_share, gdp_per_capita,
    intensity_observed = carbon_intensity
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Predicted log intensity at current coal share + own GDP per capita
    log_pred_current = predict(
      intensity_fit_multivar,
      newdata = data.frame(coal_share = coal_share,
                           gdp_per_capita = gdp_per_capita)
    ),
    # Predicted log intensity at the BENCHMARK mean coal share (own GDP/cap)
    log_pred_bench = predict(
      intensity_fit_multivar,
      newdata = data.frame(coal_share     = benchmark_mean_coal_share,
                           gdp_per_capita = gdp_per_capita)
    ),
    pred_current = exp(log_pred_current),
    pred_bench   = exp(log_pred_bench),
    # Multiplicative transition gap, comparing model predictions only
    # (not observed-vs-predicted) so the residual is held constant
    gap_pct = (1 - pred_bench / pred_current) * 100,
    # Absolute intensity reduction implied by the coal-share lever
    intensity_reduction = pred_current - pred_bench
  )

# Inline scalars for the Transition-Gap section
vietnam_gap   <- counterfactual_data |> filter(country == "Vietnam")   |> pull(gap_pct)
indonesia_gap <- counterfactual_data |> filter(country == "Indonesia") |> pull(gap_pct)
india_gap     <- counterfactual_data |> filter(country == "India")     |> pull(gap_pct)

pluck_metric <- function(cty, var) {
  latest_panel_focus |>
    filter(country == cty) |>
    pull({{ var }})
}

fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 0, signed = TRUE) {
  prefix <- if (signed && x > 0) "+" else ""
  paste0(prefix, round(x, digits), "%")
}

fmt_share <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  paste0(round(x * 100, digits), "%")
}

fmt_p <- function(x) {
  if (is.na(x)) {
    return("NA")
  }
  if (x < 0.001) {
    return("< 0.001")
  }
  sprintf("= %.3f", x)
}

report_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e5dfd4", linewidth = 0.5),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        size = 16,
        colour = "#20262a"
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(
        size = 11.5,
        colour = "#5b646b",
        margin = margin(b = 10)
      ),
      plot.caption = element_text(
        size = 8.6,
        colour = "#5b646b",
        hjust = 0
      ),
      axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#20262a"),
      axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
      axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "#3a3f44"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 2)),
      axis.text.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 3)),
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#20262a"),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#20262a"),
      legend.text = element_text(colour = "#3a3f44")
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
priority_widget_data <- priority_plot_data |>
  transmute(
    country,
    carbon_intensity = round(carbon_intensity, 1),
    growth = round(co2_growth_10yr_pct, 1),
    coal_share = round(coal_share * 100, 1),
    total_co2 = round(co2, 1),
    label_x = round(label_x, 1),
    label_y = round(label_y, 1),
    group = if_else(priority_level == "Benchmark", "benchmark", "target"),
    role = priority_level
  )

trend_widget_data <- trend_data |>
  left_join(
    latest_panel_focus |>
      transmute(country, role = priority_level),
    by = "country"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    country,
    year,
    carbon_intensity = round(carbon_intensity, 1),
    group = if_else(role == "Benchmark", "benchmark", "target")
  )

trend_endpoint_data <- trend_labels |>
  left_join(
    latest_panel_focus |>
      transmute(
        country,
        intensity_change_pct = round(intensity_change_pct, 1),
        role = priority_level
      ),
    by = "country"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    country,
    year,
    end_value = round(carbon_intensity, 1),
    label_y = round(label_y, 1),
    change = intensity_change_pct,
    group = if_else(role == "Benchmark", "benchmark", "target")
  )

fuel_widget_data <- fuel_long |>
  left_join(
    latest_panel_focus |>
      transmute(country, role = priority_level),
    by = "country"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    country = as.character(country),
    source = as.character(source),
    share = round(share * 100, 1),
    group = if_else(role == "Benchmark", "benchmark", "target")
  )

transition_widget_data <- counterfactual_data |>
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      role == "Benchmark" ~ "benchmark",
      role == "Supporting case" ~ "support",
      TRUE ~ "target"
    ),
    label = case_when(
      gap_pct >=  1 ~ sprintf("−%.0f%%", gap_pct),
      gap_pct <= -1 ~ sprintf("+%.0f%%", -gap_pct),
      TRUE          ~ "≈ 0%"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(coal_share)) |>
  transmute(
    country,
    role,
    group,
    coal_share = round(coal_share * 100, 1),
    pred_current = round(pred_current, 1),
    pred_bench = round(pred_bench, 1),
    gap_pct = round(gap_pct, 1),
    label
  )

emit_json <- function(id, x) {
  cat(
    sprintf(
      "<script id=\"%s\" type=\"application/json\">%s</script>\n",
      id,
      jsonlite::toJSON(x, auto_unbox = TRUE, dataframe = "rows", digits = 8)
    )
  )
}

emit_json(
  "priority-data",
  list(
    points = priority_widget_data,
    benchmark_mean = round(benchmark_mean_intensity, 1),
    zone = list(xmin = 180, xmax = 390, ymin = 0, ymax = 125)
  )
)

emit_json(
  "trend-data",
  list(
    series = trend_widget_data,
    endpoints = trend_endpoint_data,
    band = list(ymin = 250, ymax = 440)
  )
)

emit_json(
  "fuel-data",
  list(
    segments = fuel_widget_data,
    order = fuel_order
  )
)

emit_json(
  "transition-gap-data",
  list(
    rows = transition_widget_data,
    benchmark_mean_coal_share = round(benchmark_mean_coal_share * 100, 1)
  )
)
```

The evidence chain is strongest when the figures are read together rather than separately: Figure 1 identifies the priority zone, Figure 2 tests whether high intensity is persistent, and Figure 3 explains which partnership lever matters once a country is prioritised.

# Evidence {#sec-evidence}

Total emissions alone are not enough: China, the United States and India are the largest 2022 emitters, but prioritisation is about transition leverage, not scale. Figure 1 maps carbon intensity, 10-year CO2 growth, total CO2 and coal share. Vietnam combines `r round(pluck_metric("Vietnam", carbon_intensity))` t CO2 per million 2011 PPP$ with `r fmt_pct(pluck_metric("Vietnam", co2_growth_10yr_pct), 1)` CO2 growth; Indonesia combines `r fmt_pct(pluck_metric("Indonesia", co2_growth_10yr_pct), 1)` growth with a `r fmt_share(pluck_metric("Indonesia", coal_share), 1)` coal share; all three benchmarks record negative CO2 growth.

```{r}
#| label: code-evidence-setup
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Code — evidence setup for the main figures"
# Focus economies and benchmark labels used across Figures 1-3
focus_target    <- c("Indonesia", "Vietnam", "India")
focus_benchmark <- c("Australia", "Japan", "South Korea")
focus_all       <- c(focus_target, focus_benchmark)

# Country-level OWID rows only; OWID aggregate regions are excluded
co2_countries <- co2_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(iso_code), !str_starts(iso_code, "OWID")) |>
  mutate(
    carbon_intensity = co2 / gdp * 1e12,
    coal_share = coal_co2 / co2,
    oil_share = oil_co2 / co2,
    gas_share = gas_co2 / co2,
    cement_share = cement_co2 / co2
  )

# Ten-year growth and intensity-change summaries used in Figure 1 and the table
growth_10yr <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2022)) |>
  select(country, iso_code, year, co2) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = co2, names_prefix = "co2_") |>
  mutate(co2_growth_10yr_pct = (co2_2022 - co2_2012) / co2_2012 * 100) |>
  select(country, iso_code, co2_growth_10yr_pct)

intensity_change <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2022)) |>
  select(country, year, carbon_intensity) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = carbon_intensity,
              names_prefix = "intensity_") |>
  mutate(intensity_change_pct =
           (intensity_2022 - intensity_2012) / intensity_2012 * 100) |>
  select(country, intensity_change_pct)

# Latest complete-year panel for the report's decision map
latest_panel_all <- co2_countries |>
  filter(year == 2022, co2 > 0, gdp > 0) |>
  select(country, co2, gdp, carbon_intensity,
         coal_share, oil_share, gas_share, cement_share) |>
  left_join(growth_10yr |> select(country, co2_growth_10yr_pct), by = "country") |>
  left_join(intensity_change, by = "country")

latest_panel_focus <- latest_panel_all |>
  filter(country %in% focus_all) |>
  mutate(
    priority_level = case_when(
      country %in% c("Indonesia", "Vietnam") ~ "Primary target",
      country == "India" ~ "Supporting case",
      TRUE ~ "Benchmark"
    )
  )

# These objects feed the three interactive SVG figures in the Evidence section
priority_widget_data <- latest_panel_all |> filter(!is.na(carbon_intensity), !is.na(coal_share))
trend_widget_data    <- trend_data      |> filter(country %in% focus_all)
fuel_widget_data     <- fuel_long       |> filter(country %in% focus_all)
```

```{r}
#| label: code-figure-1-priority-map
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Code — Figure 1 priority map"
priority_widget_data <- latest_panel_all |>
  mutate(
    role = case_when(
      country %in% c("Vietnam", "Indonesia") ~ "target",
      country %in% c("Australia", "Japan", "South Korea") ~ "benchmark",
      TRUE ~ "other"
    ),
    coal_category = case_when(
      coal_share >= 0.60 ~ "High coal share",
      coal_share >= 0.30 ~ "Moderate coal share",
      TRUE ~ "Lower coal share"
    )
  )

# The document emits this object as JSON and a small JavaScript/SVG layer draws:
# x = carbon_intensity, y = 10-year CO2 growth, size = total CO2,
# fill = coal category, and buttons = all / priority / benchmark focus.
emit_json("priority-data", list(points = priority_widget_data))
```

Figure 3 identifies the relevant partnership lever. Coal still supplies `r fmt_share(pluck_metric("India", coal_share), 1)` of India's CO2, `r fmt_share(pluck_metric("Indonesia", coal_share), 1)` of Indonesia's and `r fmt_share(pluck_metric("Vietnam", coal_share), 1)` of Vietnam's, so the recommendation points toward clean-power finance, grid flexibility and coal displacement rather than generic climate diplomacy. This reading is consistent with <a class="cite-link" href="#ref-iea-seao">IEA (2024a)</a>, <a class="cite-link" href="#ref-iea-weinvest">IEA (2024b)</a>, <a class="cite-link" href="#ref-ipcc-ar6">IPCC (2022)</a> and <a class="cite-link" href="#ref-wb-phasedown">World Bank (2023)</a>.

The hypothesis test extends the sample to every country with complete 2022 data. A log-linear regression finds a positive association between coal share and carbon intensity (beta = `r round(beta1, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(beta1_p)`, n = `r nrow(reg_data)`), so the visual pattern is not just a six-country artifact. Coal share is used here as a prioritisation signal, not as sole causal proof.

Taken together, the evidence directly supports the recommendation: Vietnam and Indonesia combine the clearest priority-zone position, weaker decoupling and coal-heavy transition levers; India remains a supporting case because its coal dependence is high but its intensity trajectory is less stalled. This is a prioritisation guide, not project selection; feasibility, cost and local grid constraints still require due diligence.

# Statistical Support {#sec-statistical-support}

## Hypothesis Test {#sec-hypothesis}

To test whether coal-heavy systems are systematically more emissions-intensive, a 2022 cross-country log-linear regression models **log carbon intensity** on **coal share**. The estimated slope is **`r round(beta1, 2)`** (SE **`r round(beta1_se, 2)`**), with **t = `r round(beta1_t, 2)`**, **p `r fmt_p(beta1_p)`**, and **R-squared = `r round(r_sq, 2)`** across **`r nrow(reg_data)` countries**.

The sample is widened from the six focus economies to every country with complete 2022 data, so the slope reflects a cross-country structural pattern rather than a six-point line.

```{r}
#| label: code-hypothesis-fit
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Code — fit log-linear model on the 2022 cross-section"
# Widen to every country with complete intensity + coal share in 2022
reg_data <- latest_panel_all |>
  filter(!is.na(carbon_intensity), carbon_intensity > 0,
         !is.na(coal_share), coal_share >= 0, coal_share <= 1)

fit       <- lm(log(carbon_intensity) ~ coal_share, data = reg_data)
fit_tidy  <- broom::tidy(fit)      # coefficients, SE, t, p
fit_glance <- broom::glance(fit)   # R^2, F, df, n

# Headline slope on coal share + effect of a 10-point coal rise
beta1      <- fit_tidy |> filter(term == "coal_share") |> pull(estimate)
assoc_10pp <- (exp(beta1 * 0.10) - 1) * 100   # % change in intensity
```

<div class="metric-strip fade-section">
<div class="metric-strip__item">
<span class="metric-label"><span>Slope on</span><span>coal share</span></span>
<span class="metric-value">`r round(beta1, 2)`</span>
</div>
<div class="metric-strip__item">
<span class="metric-label"><span>Intensity effect</span><span>of a 10-point coal rise</span></span>
<span class="metric-value">`r round(assoc_10pp, 1)`%</span>
</div>
<div class="metric-strip__item">
<span class="metric-label"><span>Model</span><span>R-squared</span></span>
<span class="metric-value">`r round(r_sq, 2)`</span>
</div>
</div>

The result supports the report's main argument: **coal dependence is strongly associated with higher carbon intensity across countries**. The model R² of `r round(r_sq, 2)` indicates that coal share alone explains roughly a fifth of the cross-country variation in log carbon intensity — consistent with using coal share as a screening signal rather than as a deterministic cause. This is not causal proof, but it reinforces the practical reading of the visuals: coal-heavy economies are more likely to benefit from targeted clean-energy transition support. Full HATPC detail is provided in the Appendix.

## Transition Gap {#sec-transition-gap}

The headline slope on coal share is statistically significant — but for DCCEEW the more useful question is **how much that slope means in tonnes of CO2 per million 2011 PPP$**. The multivariate model in the Robustness Checks subsection lets us translate it into a decision-relevant counterfactual: *if a focus economy's coal share matched the three-benchmark average (`r round(benchmark_mean_coal_share*100, 0)`%, the 2022 mean of Australia, Japan and South Korea), holding its own GDP per capita fixed, what would the model predict for its carbon intensity?*

<div class="interactive-figure transition-gap-figure fade-section" data-chart="transition-gap">
```{r}
#| label: code-transition-gap
#| echo: true
#| results: hide
#| code-summary: "Code — transition-gap chart data"

ctr_plot <- transition_widget_data |>
  mutate(
    country = factor(country, levels = rev(country)),
    label_x = pmin(pred_bench, pred_current) - 6
  )

transition_x_range <- range(c(ctr_plot$pred_current, ctr_plot$pred_bench))
```
<div class="chart-header chart-header--transition">
<div class="chart-copy">
<p class="chart-eyebrow">Model Translation</p>
<h3 class="chart-title">Coal-share alignment produces double-digit modelled gaps for the primary targets</h3>
</div>
<div class="chart-legend transition-legend" aria-label="Transition-gap legend">
<span><i class="legend-dot legend-dot--filled"></i>Current</span>
<span><i class="legend-dot legend-dot--open"></i>Benchmark-share</span>
<span><i class="legend-line"></i>Gap</span>
</div>
</div>
<div class="interactive-chart transition-gap-stage" data-chart-stage="transition-gap"></div>
<p class="chart-caption"><strong>Transition-gap chart.</strong> Filled point: predicted carbon intensity at each focus economy's 2022 coal share. Open point: predicted intensity if coal share moved to the three-benchmark mean (about `r round(benchmark_mean_coal_share*100, 0)`% — the mean of Australia 38.0%, Japan 40.4% and South Korea 44.5%), holding GDP per capita fixed. Both points are model predictions, so each country's residual (its deviation from the world fit) is held constant; the gap therefore reflects only the coal-share lever, not observed intensity. "Tonnes CO2" means metric tonnes of carbon dioxide; PPP$ means purchasing-power-parity dollars, here constant 2011 international dollars in OWID's GDP series.</p>
</div>

The model implies the largest single-variable intensity-reduction lever for **India** (**−`r round(india_gap, 0)`%**), consistent with India's coal share being the highest in the focus group and therefore the furthest from the benchmark reference. **Indonesia** sits in the middle (**−`r round(indonesia_gap, 0)`%**), and **Vietnam** at **−`r round(vietnam_gap, 0)`%** — proportional to each country's distance from the `r round(benchmark_mean_coal_share*100, 0)`% benchmark coal share. The **benchmarks themselves** show ≈ 0% gaps because their 2022 coal shares are already at or near this reference value, which validates the construction of the metric: countries that already look like the benchmark have nothing to close. This does **not** automatically make India the first-order target, because the recommendation weighs a bundle of signals rather than the largest modelled coal-gap alone; Vietnam and Indonesia still combine weaker decoupling with a more focused Southeast Asian partnership setting. This priority framing also reflects DCCEEW's existing Southeast-Asia partnership focus under the DFAT Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040 (<a class="cite-link" href="#ref-dfat-invested">[4]</a>), within which India enters as an indispensable South-Asian comparator rather than the primary deployment target.

Read the chart as a **directional indicator**, not a forecast. The gap is the model-implied effect of moving *only one input* — coal share — to a reference value, ceteris paribus. In reality, moving coal share also moves capital stock, employment, grid composition and policy; none of those second-order effects appear here. The chart answers a narrow question — *how much intensity reduction is encoded in coal-share targeting alone?* — and leaves feasibility, finance cost and political economy to the partnership-design stage.

What this adds to the recommendation: even on the most conservative reading (where the model captures only one structural channel), coal-share-led partnership support has a **double-digit** intensity-reduction signature for both primary targets. That justifies the priority call on *quantitative* terms, not just on level / trend / coal-share triangulation. In partnership-design terms, this means the same coal-share intervention is modelled to deliver a larger per-country intensity reduction in Vietnam and Indonesia than in already-decoupled economies — the structural argument for concentrating partnership effort where the structural lever is largest.

## Robustness Checks {#sec-robustness}

The headline regression in the Hypothesis Test subsection uses one predictor on a 2022 cross-section. Three further models test whether the **coal-intensity signal** still appears under different lenses on the same OWID data. Each is a *robustness check*, not a causal proof: the report continues to read coal share as a **priority signal**, not a single decisive cause.

::: {.panel-tabset .robustness-tabs}

### Growth model

Tests whether **10-year CO2 growth (2012–2022)** still tracks **2022 coal share** once **10-year GDP growth** is netted out — i.e. whether coal-heavy economies grow emissions faster *after* accounting for the fact that they may also grow GDP faster.

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: tbl-growth-fit
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Growth model: CO2 growth (%, 2012–2022) regressed on 2022 coal share and GDP growth (%, 2012–2022)."
growth_fit_tidy |>
  transmute(
    Term = case_when(
      term == "(Intercept)"           ~ "Intercept",
      term == "coal_share"            ~ "Coal share (2022)",
      term == "gdp_growth_10yr_pct"   ~ "GDP growth, 2012–2022 (%)",
      TRUE                            ~ term
    ),
    Estimate     = signif(estimate, 3),
    `Std. error` = signif(std.error, 3),
    `t-stat`     = signif(statistic, 3),
    `p-value`    = signif(p.value, 3),
    `CI 2.5%`    = signif(conf.low, 3),
    `CI 97.5%`   = signif(conf.high, 3)
  ) |>
  kable(format = "html", table.attr = "class='summary-table'")
```
</div>

After controlling for GDP growth, the coal-share coefficient is **`r round(growth_coal_beta, 1)`** but **not statistically significant** (p `r fmt_p(growth_coal_p)`); the GDP-growth control is the dominant predictor (β = **`r round(growth_gdp_beta, 2)`**, p `r fmt_p(growth_gdp_p)`), with model R² = `r round(growth_r_sq, 2)` on `r nrow(growth_model_data)` countries. **The honest read: decade-on-decade CO2 growth is largely a GDP-growth story, not a pure coal-share story.** Coal share matters most for *how much CO2 each unit of GDP produces* (intensity, tested in the next two models) rather than for the absolute *rate of growth*. The Priority Map's vertical axis should therefore be read as a development-trajectory signal, not as direct evidence that coal share drives growth.

### Intensity-change model

Tests whether countries that **raised** coal share between 2012 and 2022 also saw their **carbon intensity rise** over the same window. Reading change-on-change instead of level-on-level partly differences out time-invariant country effects (geography, baseline industrial structure).

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: tbl-change-fit
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Intensity-change model: Δ carbon intensity (%, 2012–2022) regressed on Δ coal share (pp, 2012–2022)."
change_fit_tidy |>
  transmute(
    Term = case_when(
      term == "(Intercept)"            ~ "Intercept",
      term == "coal_share_change_pp"   ~ "Δ coal share (pp, 2012–2022)",
      TRUE                             ~ term
    ),
    Estimate     = signif(estimate, 3),
    `Std. error` = signif(std.error, 3),
    `t-stat`     = signif(statistic, 3),
    `p-value`    = signif(p.value, 3),
    `CI 2.5%`    = signif(conf.low, 3),
    `CI 97.5%`   = signif(conf.high, 3)
  ) |>
  kable(format = "html", table.attr = "class='summary-table'")
```
</div>

A 1-percentage-point rise in coal share over the decade is associated with a **`r round(change_coal_beta, 2)`%** change in carbon intensity (p `r fmt_p(change_coal_p)`, R² = `r round(change_r_sq, 2)`, n = `r nrow(intensity_change_model_data)`). The effect is statistically strong and in the expected direction: countries that grew their coal share also saw intensity rise (or fall less). Because differences-on-differences partially absorb time-invariant country effects, this is the most robust of the three checks for the headline coal–intensity link. Still associational — strong directional evidence, not a causal coefficient.

### Multivariate intensity model

Tests whether the **coal-share slope on log carbon intensity** survives once **log GDP per capita** is added as a control for development level. Many low-coal economies are also high-income service economies, so the headline univariate slope partly reflects this confound.

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: tbl-mv-fit
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Multivariate intensity model: log(carbon intensity, 2022) regressed on coal share and log(GDP per capita, 2022)."
intensity_fit_multivar_tidy |>
  transmute(
    Term = case_when(
      term == "(Intercept)"          ~ "Intercept",
      term == "coal_share"           ~ "Coal share (2022)",
      term == "log(gdp_per_capita)"  ~ "log GDP per capita (2022)",
      TRUE                           ~ term
    ),
    Estimate     = signif(estimate, 3),
    `Std. error` = signif(std.error, 3),
    `t-stat`     = signif(statistic, 3),
    `p-value`    = signif(p.value, 3),
    `CI 2.5%`    = signif(conf.low, 3),
    `CI 97.5%`   = signif(conf.high, 3)
  ) |>
  kable(format = "html", table.attr = "class='summary-table'")
```
</div>

After adding log GDP per capita as a control, the coal-share slope is essentially unchanged: **`r round(mv_coal_beta, 2)`** versus the univariate **`r round(beta1, 2)`**, still highly significant (p `r fmt_p(mv_coal_p)`, model R² = `r round(mv_r_sq, 2)`). The log GDP-per-capita coefficient is small (**`r round(mv_gdpcap_beta, 2)`**) and **not statistically significant** (p `r fmt_p(mv_gdpcap_p)`), suggesting that — within this linear specification — development level does not absorb additional variation in log carbon intensity once coal share is in the model. The coal signal therefore **survives the development control** rather than being explained away by the fact that wealthier economies happen to use less coal. This is the cleanest robustness result of the three: the headline coal–intensity association is not an artifact of conflating coal use with national income.

### What the three checks together support

The three checks tell a consistent — but more nuanced — story than the headline regression alone. Coal share is **positively signed in all three specifications** and **statistically significant in two of three** (intensity-change and multivariate); it is **not significant** for decade-on-decade *growth* once GDP growth is controlled for. Read together:

- **Coal share is a robust signal for carbon intensity** (level and change). Its slope on log intensity barely moves when development level is added, and its decade-on-decade *change* tracks the change in intensity strongly.
- **Coal share is not, on its own, a robust signal for emissions growth**. Decade-on-decade growth is dominated by GDP growth itself, so the Priority Map's growth axis should be read as a development-trajectory marker rather than as separate evidence of a coal effect.

Together the checks support reading coal share as a **priority indicator** for *what kind of partnership lever fits* (clean-power transition, grid flexibility), but they discipline the report against treating coal share as a one-cause explanation for emissions growth. The claims remain **associational** — robustness checks, not causal proof.

:::

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

<div class="fade-section">
<ol class="limitation-list">
<li><strong>OWID is mainly production-based.</strong> The dataset measures territorial emissions, so it does not fully capture consumption-based responsibility or emissions embodied in trade. This matters when comparing developing production economies with higher-income consumption economies.<a class="cite-link" href="#ref-peters">[5]</a> Conversely, this strengthens rather than weakens the case for partnership support: helping Vietnam and Indonesia decarbonise production also reduces the embodied carbon flowing into Australian and broader Indo-Pacific supply chains, an effect not visible in the territorial accounting used here.</li>
<li><strong>Country averages hide project detail.</strong> National data cannot identify the provinces, sectors, grid constraints or financing windows where partnership support would land. The report prioritises <em>countries</em>, not specific investments.</li>
<li><strong>The statistical evidence is associational.</strong> Coal share, carbon intensity and CO2 growth move together in useful ways, but the models do not prove that coal share alone <em>causes</em> higher intensity. Industrial structure, technology, regulation, energy prices and GDP growth also shape the results.</li>
<li><strong>Priority is not feasibility.</strong> A high coal share signals both transition leverage and transition difficulty: embedded capital stock, employment exposure and grid design can make clean-energy support slower or more expensive. DCCEEW would still need country-level due diligence before designing projects.</li>
</ol>
</div>

# Appendix {#sec-appendix}

Detailed diagnostics, full HATPC reporting and supplementary robustness visuals are collected here so the main report can stay reader-focused without losing analytical transparency.

## Appendix 1 — HATPC Process {#sec-appendix1}

Full Hypotheses / Assumptions / Test statistic / P-value / Conclusion (HATPC) detail for the log-linear regression used in the Hypothesis Test subsection.

::: {.panel-tabset .hatpc-tabs}

### H

**H — Hypotheses**

- **H0:** The slope on coal share is zero; coal dependence has no linear association with log carbon intensity.
- **H1:** The slope on coal share is not zero; coal dependence is associated with log carbon intensity.

### A

**A — Assumptions**

- **Linearity:** The fitted log-linear form is appropriate as a first-order approximation for the cross-country relationship.
- **Normality:** Residuals are approximately normal after log transformation; Shapiro-Wilk **p `r fmt_p(shapiro_p)`**.
- **Independence:** Each observation is a distinct country in the 2022 cross-section.
- **Scope:** The model is descriptive and cross-sectional, so it supports prioritisation rather than causal inference.

The two diagnostic panels below back up the linearity and normality claims visually. The residuals-vs-fitted plot should show no obvious curvature or fan shape; the normal Q-Q plot should track the diagonal reference line.

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: fig-diag
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Residuals vs fitted log carbon intensity. A flat smoother and roughly even spread support the linearity / equal-variance assumptions."
#|   - "Normal Q-Q of standardised residuals. Points hugging the diagonal support the normality assumption used by the t / F inference."
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.8
fit_aug <- broom::augment(fit) |>
  mutate(.std_resid = .resid / sd(.resid, na.rm = TRUE))

# Residuals vs fitted
ggplot(fit_aug, aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             colour = "#6c665d", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = "#945638", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE,
              colour = "#5b646b", linewidth = 0.7, span = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Fitted log(carbon intensity)",
       y = "Residual") +
  report_theme()

# Normal Q-Q of standardised residuals
ggplot(fit_aug, aes(sample = .std_resid)) +
  stat_qq(colour = "#945638", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#5b646b", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles",
       y = "Standardised residual") +
  report_theme()
```
</div>

The smoother in the residuals plot is roughly flat with no funnel shape, and the Q-Q points track the diagonal closely except for a few mild tail outliers — the inferential statistics in the Hypothesis Test subsection (β₁, p-value, R²) can therefore be read in the usual way without major caveats.

### T

**T — Test Statistic**

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit_tidy |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Regression coefficients.")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit_glance |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, statistic, df, df.residual, p.value, nobs) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ signif(.x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Model summary.")
```

### P

**P — P-value**

The p-value for the coal-share slope is **`r fmt_p(beta1_p)`**, so the null hypothesis is rejected.

### C

**C — Conclusion**

There is strong evidence of a positive association between coal dependence and carbon intensity in the 2022 cross-section. This supports the report's recommendation logic, while still stopping short of causal interpretation.

:::

### Data and Reproducibility Notes

- All aggregate rows with missing `iso_code` or `iso_code` beginning with `OWID` were excluded.
- 2022 was used as the latest year with complete GDP coverage for the focus economies.
- Carbon intensity is defined as `co2 / gdp * 10^12`, giving tonnes of CO2 per million **2011 international (PPP) dollars** of GDP — OWID's `gdp` column is the Maddison Project series, not market-exchange-rate USD.
- Ten-year CO2 growth is defined as `(CO2_2022 - CO2_2012) / CO2_2012`.
- Latest-year evidence was combined with 2012-2022 trend information to avoid over-relying on a single-year snapshot.
- **Sample composition transparency**: of the `r n_2022_country_rows` country-rows present in OWID for 2022, `r n_panel_all` had complete `carbon_intensity`, `coal_share` and `co2`; the headline regression in the Hypothesis Test subsection then drops a further `r n_dropped_to_reg` rows that fail the regression filters (non-positive intensity or out-of-range coal share), leaving **n = `r n_reg_data`** countries.

A small set of formatting helpers and a custom ggplot theme keep the inline numbers and every figure stylistically consistent across the report:

```{r}
#| label: code-appendix-helpers
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Code — formatting helpers and report_theme()"
# Pull a single metric for a focus country (used in inline numbers)
pluck_metric <- function(cty, var) {
  latest_panel_focus |> filter(country == cty) |> pull({{ var }})
}

# Signed percentage with a fixed number of digits, e.g. "+14%"
fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 0, signed = TRUE) {
  prefix <- if (signed && x > 0) "+" else ""
  paste0(prefix, round(x, digits), "%")
}

# Shared ggplot theme — warm paper background, muted gridlines
report_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e5dfd4", linewidth = 0.5),
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, colour = "#20262a"),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 11.5, colour = "#5b646b"),
      axis.title       = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#20262a"),
      axis.title.x     = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
      axis.title.y     = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
      axis.text        = element_text(colour = "#3a3f44"),
      axis.text.x      = element_text(margin = margin(t = 2)),
      axis.text.y      = element_text(margin = margin(r = 3)),
      legend.position  = "top"
    )
}
```

### Small multiples: intensity 1990→2022

<p class="chart-caption"><strong>Appendix diagnostic.</strong> Carbon intensity trajectories for the six focus economies, 1990-2022. The vertical reference line marks the 2012 baseline used in the report; Vietnam and Indonesia show flatter or rising tails while the benchmark economies bend downward.</p>
</div>

Each facet uses its own y-axis so individual shape is legible. The key signal is the **direction** at the 2012 line: Vietnam and Indonesia have flat-to-rising tails, while the three benchmark economies bend downward.

### Focus six on the world fit

This view places the six focus economies on the same regression line used in the Hypothesis Test subsection (`log(carbon_intensity) ~ coal_share`, n = `r nrow(reg_data)` countries). It bridges the country-specific narrative and the cross-country statistical pattern — if the focus six sit broadly along the world fit, the headline coal-intensity claim is internally consistent.

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: code-world-fit
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 5.8
focus_world_data <- reg_data |>
  mutate(
    log_intensity = log(carbon_intensity),
    is_focus = country %in% c("Indonesia", "Vietnam", "India",
                              "Australia", "Japan", "South Korea"),
    role = case_when(
      country %in% c("Indonesia", "Vietnam") ~ "Primary target",
      country == "India"                     ~ "Supporting case",
      country %in% c("Australia", "Japan",
                     "South Korea")          ~ "Benchmark",
      TRUE                                   ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

# Fixed label positions keep the crowded middle of the chart readable.
focus_world_label_positions <- tribble(
  ~country,        ~label_x, ~label_y, ~label_hjust,
  "Vietnam",          0.64,     6.17,          0,
  "Indonesia",        0.47,     5.22,          1,
  "India",            0.76,     6.20,          0,
  "Australia",        0.35,     5.28,          1,
  "Japan",            0.29,     5.10,        0.5,
  "South Korea",      0.45,     6.06,        0.5
)

focus_world_six_lab <- focus_world_data |>
  filter(is_focus) |>
  left_join(focus_world_label_positions, by = "country")

ggplot(focus_world_data, aes(coal_share, log_intensity)) +
  geom_point(data = focus_world_data |> filter(!is_focus),
             colour = "#c9c0b0", size = 1.7, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              colour = "#945638", fill = "#e8d6bf",
              alpha = 0.40, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = focus_world_data |> filter(is_focus),
             aes(colour = role), size = 3.6) +
  geom_segment(data = focus_world_six_lab,
               aes(x = coal_share, y = log_intensity,
                   xend = label_x, yend = label_y),
               colour = "#5b646b", linewidth = 0.32,
               alpha = 0.74, lineend = "round") +
  geom_text(data = focus_world_six_lab,
            aes(x = label_x, y = label_y,
                label = country, colour = role, hjust = label_hjust),
            size = 3.15, fontface = "plain",
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    `Primary target`    = "#c87638",
    `Supporting case`   = "#b08a3a",
    Benchmark           = "#7b8d9f"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    x = "Coal share of national CO2, 2022",
    y = "log(carbon intensity, t CO2 / million 2011 PPP$)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  report_theme() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.title = element_text(face = "plain", colour = "#5b646b"),
    axis.title.x = element_text(face = "plain", colour = "#5b646b",
                                margin = margin(t = 12)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(face = "plain", colour = "#5b646b",
                                margin = margin(r = 12)),
    legend.text = element_text(colour = "#3a3f44")
  )
```
<p class="chart-caption"><strong>Appendix diagnostic.</strong> Focus six placed on the global coal-share / log(carbon-intensity) fit. Grey points: all OWID countries with complete 2022 data. Orange line: the headline univariate OLS, with 95% confidence ribbon. Coloured points: the six focus economies labelled by priority role.</p>
</div>

The fitted line slopes upward, confirming that countries with higher coal shares tend to have higher log carbon intensities. **Vietnam** sits clearly above the world fit — more carbon-intensive than its coal share alone would predict — which sharpens the case for it as a primary target. **Indonesia** sits close to the line, and **India** sits slightly below the line despite the highest coal share in the focus group, consistent with India's faster-improving intensity trajectory. **Australia, Japan and South Korea** cluster around or below the line at moderate coal shares, in line with their benchmark role. The six are spread across the world pattern rather than bunched in a corner — supporting the report's reading that the recommendation reflects a broader cross-country relationship, not a feature of just six points.

### Pre-COVID growth (2010 → 2019)

The headline growth window (2012 → 2022) spans the COVID-19 demand shock. A reasonable objection — especially against Vietnam's **+`r round(pluck_metric("Vietnam", co2_growth_10yr_pct), 0)`%** decade growth — is that part of the figure could be a 2020–21 rebound effect rather than steady carbon-intensive expansion. This tab repeats the growth comparison on a strictly pre-COVID window (2010 → 2019).

<div class="fade-section">
```{r}
#| label: code-precovid-growth
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 4.6
precovid_long <- focus_growth_compare |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(growth_2012_2022, co2_growth_precovid_pct),
    names_to  = "window",
    values_to = "growth_pct"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    window = recode(window,
                    growth_2012_2022          = "2012–2022 (headline, includes COVID)",
                    co2_growth_precovid_pct   = "2010–2019 (pre-COVID)"),
    window = factor(window,
                    levels = c("2012–2022 (headline, includes COVID)",
                               "2010–2019 (pre-COVID)"))
  )

# Order countries by the headline window so both panels share the same y-order
country_order <- focus_growth_compare |>
  arrange(desc(growth_2012_2022)) |>
  pull(country)

precovid_long <- precovid_long |>
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = rev(country_order)))

ggplot(precovid_long,
       aes(x = growth_pct, y = country, fill = role)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.68) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#6c665d", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%+.0f%%", growth_pct),
        hjust = ifelse(growth_pct >= 0, -0.12, 1.12)),
    size = 3.3, colour = "#18384a"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ window, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    `Primary target` = "#c87638",
    `Supporting case` = "#b08a3a",
    Benchmark        = "#7b8d9f"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1, accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.14, 0.20))
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  report_theme() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.spacing   = unit(1.4, "lines"),
    strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#18384a", size = 10.8),
    axis.text.x     = element_text(colour = "#5b646b")
  )
```
<p class="chart-caption"><strong>Appendix diagnostic.</strong> Ten-year CO2 growth under the headline 2012-2022 window and the pre-COVID 2010-2019 window. Both windows keep Vietnam, Indonesia and India on the growth side, while Australia, Japan and South Korea remain flat or declining.</p>
</div>

**The result runs in the opposite direction to the standard objection**: the pre-COVID 2010–2019 window shows **larger** decade growth for every focus economy, not smaller. Vietnam's number rises from +`r round(pluck_metric("Vietnam", co2_growth_10yr_pct), 0)`% to +`r round(focus_growth_compare |> filter(country == "Vietnam") |> pull(co2_growth_precovid_pct), 0)`%, India from +`r round(pluck_metric("India", co2_growth_10yr_pct), 0)`% to +`r round(focus_growth_compare |> filter(country == "India") |> pull(co2_growth_precovid_pct), 0)`%, and the benchmarks shift from declines to near-flat. **COVID dampened the apparent growth of carbon-intensive economies; it did not inflate them.** The qualitative ranking — Vietnam > India ≈ Indonesia ≫ {Australia, Japan, South Korea} — holds in both windows, so the priority call is robust to the choice of growth window. If anything, the headline 2012–2022 figures *understate* Vietnam's underlying carbon-intensive trajectory.
